name: Karbala
tagline: The shrine city of Imam Husayn, heart of Shia pilgrimage
summary: Karbala is where Imam Husayn, grandson of the Prophet Muhammad, was killed in 680, and his golden-domed shrine is one of the most visited places on earth. Pilgrims come all year, and in their millions for Ashura and Arbaeen, when many walk here from Najaf. Check your government's current travel advice for Iraq before planning.
seasonNote: Ashura and Arbaeen follow the Islamic calendar and move about 11 days earlier each year; Arbaeen draws 20 million or more and hotels fill months ahead. Summer passes 48°C, so winter is the comfortable time to visit.
arrival: Many governments advise against some or all travel to Iraq; read yours first. Fly to Najaf (about 80 km) or Baghdad (about 100 km), then take a taxi or shared car. Many nationalities can get a visa online or on arrival, and visas are often waived for Arbaeen pilgrims.
gettingAround: The two shrines and the souks between them are all walkable; vehicles are kept out of the centre. Use taxis or a driver for the desert sights.
cashTip: Iraq runs on cash. Bring clean US dollar notes and change them for dinars; ATMs that take foreign cards are few.
foodTip: Eat where pilgrims eat: kebab and tikka from the grills around the shrines, kahi pastry with geymar cream for breakfast, and the free food (nazri) handed out on holy days.
buyTip: Prayer beads, turbah prayer stones made from Karbala's soil, rosewater, shrine-made textiles and dates.
baseArea: The hotels between the two shrines, along Bayn al-Haramayn and the streets just off it

connections.note: Flights land in Najaf or Baghdad, then about 90 minutes by road.

items.name: Imam Husayn Shrine
items.summary: The golden-domed shrine over the tomb of Imam Husayn, with mirror-tiled halls and courtyards that never empty.
items.expect: Security checks and shoe drops at every gate; women wear an abaya or chador, which can be borrowed. Non-Muslim visitors are usually welcome in the courtyards when dressed modestly.
items.tip: Come before dawn or late at night, when the courtyards are calm and the dome glows.
items.why: One of the holiest sites in Shia Islam.
flow: Leave shoes and bags at the gate stores.
Walk the courtyard, then on to Al-Abbas across Bayn al-Haramayn.

items.name: Al-Abbas Shrine
items.summary: The shrine of Abbas ibn Ali, Husayn's half-brother and standard-bearer, facing Husayn's shrine across the plaza.
items.expect: The same entry rules as the Husayn shrine; busiest at evening prayers.
items.tip: Its museum of gifts given to the shrine over the centuries is worth an hour.
items.why: The second great shrine of Karbala.
flow: Courtyard, then the museum if open.

items.name: Bayn al-Haramayn
items.summary: The wide plaza joining the two shrines, where pilgrims walk back and forth between them.
items.expect: Packed at dusk and on holy days; shaded in parts.
items.tip: Stand in the middle at sunset to see both domes lit at once.
items.why: The best view in the city, and the walk every pilgrim makes.

items.name: Tal al-Zaynabiya
items.summary: The small hill beside Husayn's shrine where, by tradition, his sister Zaynab watched the battle.
items.expect: A small shrine room; often crowded with women pilgrims.
items.tip: Pair it with your visit to the Husayn shrine; it is a minute's walk.
items.why: A moving part of the Karbala story.
flow: Exit the Husayn shrine on its west side.

items.name: Al-Ukhaidir Fortress
items.summary: A vast 8th-century Abbasid palace-fortress of brick vaults and arches standing alone in the desert.
items.expect: Little shade and few facilities; you need a driver.
items.tip: Go early morning and bring water; combine with Lake Razzaza on the way back.
items.why: One of the finest early Islamic buildings anywhere.
flow: Walk the courtyards and vaulted halls.

items.name: Karbala souks
items.summary: Covered markets ringing the shrines, selling prayer stones, beads, cloth and sweets.
items.expect: Busy and loud; prices are often fixed for pilgrims.
items.tip: Look for turbah prayer stones made from local soil, a gift pilgrims take home.
items.why: Where the city's daily life happens around its shrines.
flow: Start at the Husayn shrine's gates.

items.name: Shrine-side kebab grills
items.summary: Rows of grills turning out Iraqi kebab and tikka with flatbread, onions and sumac.
items.expect: Simple seating; food comes fast.
items.tip: Order by the skewer and share; ask for amba mango pickle.
items.why: The everyday meal of Karbala's pilgrims.
flow: Eat at the counter or take it away.

items.name: Kahi and geymar breakfast
items.summary: Flaky kahi pastry with thick buffalo cream and date syrup, Iraq's favourite breakfast.
items.expect: Morning only; sells out.
items.tip: Go straight after dawn prayers.
items.why: The Iraqi breakfast to try.
flow: Find a kahi shop near the shrines.

items.name: Masgouf by the river
items.summary: Carp split and slow-grilled upright beside a wood fire, Iraq's national dish.
items.expect: Takes 45 minutes or more; you pick your fish.
items.tip: Order before you sit down and share one fish between two or three.
items.why: The dish Iraqis are proudest of.

name: Najaf · Kufa
tagline: Imam Ali's shrine and the world's largest cemetery
summary: Najaf holds the shrine of Ali ibn Abi Talib, cousin and son-in-law of the Prophet Muhammad and the first Shia Imam, and is the centre of Shia scholarship. Beside it lies Wadi al-Salam, perhaps the largest cemetery on earth, and nearby Kufa has one of Islam's oldest mosques. Check your government's current travel advice for Iraq before planning.
seasonNote: Busiest around Arbaeen, when pilgrims set out on foot for Karbala (about 80 km over two or three days), and on Eid al-Ghadir. Summer passes 48°C.
arrival: Many governments advise against some or all travel to Iraq; read yours first. Najaf International Airport has flights from Dubai, Istanbul, Tehran and the Gulf, about 30 minutes from the shrine. Many nationalities can get a visa online or on arrival.
gettingAround: The old city around the shrine is walkable. Taxis are cheap for Kufa (about 10 km) and the cemetery's far sections.
cashTip: Cash-based like the rest of Iraq; bring clean US dollar notes to change for dinars.
foodTip: Najaf's old souk is lined with kebab grills, bakeries and sweet shops; try the local dates and the sweet halawa.
buyTip: Najaf is known for prayer beads, agate rings, religious books and fine cloaks (aba) worn by clerics.
baseArea: The hotels in the old city near the Imam Ali Shrine

connections.note: Taxi or shared car; at Arbaeen, millions walk it.

items.name: Imam Ali Shrine
items.summary: The golden-domed shrine over the tomb of Imam Ali, with mirror mosaics and a courtyard full of pilgrims day and night.
items.expect: Security checks and shoe drops at the gates; women wear an abaya or chador. Respectful non-Muslim visitors are usually welcome in the courtyard.
items.tip: The shrine's museum of treasures given over a thousand years is worth seeing if open.
items.why: One of the holiest sites in Shia Islam.
flow: Enter through the Bab al-Qibla gate.

items.name: Wadi al-Salam cemetery
items.summary: A city of tombs and domes stretching for kilometres, where millions of Muslims have been buried to lie near Imam Ali; it includes shrines of the prophets Hud and Salih.
items.expect: Vast and easy to get lost in; go with a guide or driver.
items.tip: Visit the shrine of Hud and Salih inside it, and go in the cool of late afternoon.
items.why: One of the largest cemeteries in the world, and a deeply moving place.
flow: Start from the old city's northern edge.
A driver can take you to the prophets' shrines.

items.name: Great Mosque of Kufa
items.summary: One of the oldest mosques in the world, where Imam Ali led prayers and was struck down in 661.
items.expect: Large open courtyard with small shrines in its corners.
items.tip: Visit Ali's house next door, where he lived as caliph.
items.why: Fourteen centuries of history in one courtyard.
flow: Mosque, then the house of Ali beside it.

items.name: Al-Sahla Mosque
items.summary: An early mosque in Kufa associated with several prophets, where pilgrims gather on Tuesday nights.
items.expect: Calm by day, crowded on Tuesday evenings.
items.tip: Combine with the Great Mosque of Kufa in one trip.
items.why: One of the most revered mosques for Shia pilgrims.
flow: A short taxi from the Kufa mosque.

items.name: Najaf old souk
items.summary: The great covered market running from the shrine, with stalls of rings, beads, books, sweets and cloth.
items.expect: Narrow, busy and shaded.
items.tip: Look for agate rings and the cloaks clerics wear.
items.why: The life of the city between prayers.
flow: Start at the shrine's eastern gate.

items.name: Kufa riverside
items.summary: The banks of the Euphrates at Kufa, where families picnic at dusk.
items.expect: Simple cafés and boats; liveliest on Thursday and Friday evenings.
items.tip: Come at sunset after visiting the Kufa mosques.
items.why: A breath of green after the desert.
flow: Walk down from the Kufa mosque area.

items.name: Old souk kebab grills
items.summary: Grill stalls serving kebab, tikka and liver skewers wrapped in fresh samoon bread.
items.expect: Fast, cheap and crowded after prayers.
items.tip: Ask for the bread straight from the oven.
items.why: The quickest good meal in Najaf.
flow: Eat standing or on plastic stools.

items.name: Iraqi bakeries and samoon
items.summary: Diamond-shaped samoon bread baked in clay ovens, eaten hot with cheese, eggs or falafel.
items.expect: Mornings and evenings; a few coins a loaf.
items.tip: Pair it with falafel and amba from a street stall.
items.why: Iraq's everyday bread, best straight from the oven.
flow: Find a bakery with a queue.
Buy hot and eat on the walk.

items.name: Dates and halawa sweet shops
items.summary: Shops selling Iraqi dates by the kilo, halawa, baklava and date-filled kleicha biscuits.
items.expect: Tasting is usually welcome.
items.tip: Kleicha travel well and make a good gift.
items.why: Iraq grows some of the world's finest dates.
flow: Buy a box for the road.

name: Mashhad
tagline: Iran's holiest city, around the vast shrine of Imam Reza
summary: Mashhad grew up around the tomb of Imam Reza, the eighth Shia Imam, and his shrine is one of the largest mosque complexes in the world, with courtyards, museums and the 15th-century Goharshad Mosque. Over 20 million pilgrims come each year. Many governments advise against all travel to Iran; check yours before planning, and note dual nationals face extra risk.
seasonNote: Spring and autumn are mild. Nowruz (around 21 March) and summer holidays bring the biggest domestic crowds; winters are cold. Religious dates follow the Islamic calendar.
arrival: Many governments advise against all travel to Iran; read yours first, and check visa rules for your nationality. Mashhad airport has flights from Tehran (about 90 minutes), Dubai, Istanbul and the Gulf; overnight trains run from Tehran.
gettingAround: Metro line 1 runs from the airport to the shrine; taxis and the Snapp ride app are cheap. The shrine area is walkable.
cashTip: Foreign bank cards do not work in Iran, so bring all your money as euros or US dollars in cash and change it at exchange offices. Prices are often quoted in toman (1 toman = 10 rials).
foodTip: Mashhad is known for shishlik lamb chops (best in the hill villages of Torqabeh and Shandiz), sholeh mashhadi stew, and saffron and barberries from Khorasan.
buyTip: Saffron, barberries, turquoise from nearby Nishapur, prayer beads and Persian rugs.
baseArea: The hotels around the Imam Reza shrine, especially Imam Reza Street

items.name: Imam Reza shrine
items.summary: A vast complex of golden domes, tiled courtyards and mirror halls around the tomb of Imam Reza.
items.expect: Bags and cameras checked at the gates; women must wear a chador, lent at the entrances. Non-Muslims can visit the courtyards and museums, usually with a free guide from the international pilgrims office; the inner sanctum is for Muslims only.
items.tip: Ask at the gate for the foreign pilgrims office, whose volunteer guides explain each courtyard.
items.why: One of the largest and most beautiful shrines in the Islamic world.
flow: Enter through a main gate and ask for the foreign pilgrims office.
Courtyards, Goharshad Mosque, then the museums.
items.best: Evening, when the courtyards are lit

items.name: Goharshad Mosque
items.summary: A 15th-century Timurid mosque inside the shrine complex, built by Queen Goharshad, with superb blue tilework.
items.expect: Same entry rules as the shrine.
items.tip: Look up at the great iwan's tile mosaics in morning light.
items.why: A masterpiece of Timurid architecture.
flow: Reach it from the shrine courtyards.

items.name: Tomb of Nader Shah
items.summary: A modern stone memorial and museum to the 18th-century conqueror Nader Shah, with weapons and armour from his campaigns.
items.expect: Small museum; quick visit.
items.tip: Walk here from the shrine along Imam Reza Street.
items.why: A window on Iran's last great conqueror.

items.name: Kooh Sangi Park
items.summary: A rocky hill park where families climb for views over the city and picnic by the water.
items.expect: Busy on Thursday and Friday evenings.
items.tip: Climb the rocks at sunset for the city view.
items.why: The favourite local evening out.
flow: Climb, then tea in the park.

items.name: Tomb of Ferdowsi, Tus
items.summary: The mausoleum of Ferdowsi, author of the Shahnameh, Iran's national epic, in a garden at ancient Tus.
items.expect: A garden, the tomb and a small museum with Shahnameh reliefs.
items.tip: Combine with the Haruniyeh dome nearby.
items.why: The resting place of Persian literature's founding poet.

items.name: Torqabeh and Shandiz villages
items.summary: Hill villages west of the city with orchards, craft shops and garden restaurants famous for shishlik.
items.expect: Busy on weekends and in summer.
items.tip: Go in the late afternoon and stay for a shishlik dinner.
items.why: Cool air and Mashhad's best-loved meal.
items.best: Late afternoon in spring or summer

items.name: Shishlik in the garden restaurants
items.summary: Saffron-marinated lamb chops grilled over charcoal, served with rice or bread in garden restaurants.
items.expect: Large portions; tables on carpeted platforms.
items.tip: Order shishlik with saffron rice and doogh, the salty yoghurt drink.
items.why: The dish Mashhad is known for across Iran.

items.name: Sholeh mashhadi
items.summary: A thick stew of wheat, lentils, beans and meat, Mashhad's own comfort food.
items.expect: Simple shops near the shrine; best in the morning.
items.tip: Ask for it with crispy onions and mint oil.
items.why: The city's signature dish.
flow: Find a sholeh shop off Imam Reza Street.

items.name: Saffron and sweets at Bazaar Reza
items.summary: A long covered bazaar near the shrine selling saffron, barberries, nuts, nougat and saffron brittle.
items.expect: Huge and busy; compare prices.
items.tip: Buy saffron as whole threads in sealed packs, and try sohan saffron brittle.
items.why: Khorasan grows most of the world's saffron.
flow: Walk in from the shrine side.
